## Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how `clusterComposer` can be applied using three example areas in Guatemala City.

The example areas represent different urban layouts:

- **Section A:** a regular road network layout with buildings arranged in clearly defined blocks;
- **Section B:** buildings arranged in a regular pattern within a more irregular road network;
- **Section C:** an irregular layout with variation in building size and arrangement; and

For each example we use two GeoPackage files:

- a section boundary, these are saved in the format: `sectionA.gpkg`; and
- a building-level population dataset, these are saved in the format: `bfsA.gpkg`.

The example files are stored in the `clusterComposer` package's `inst/extdata` directory.

The pre-prepared section boundaries were created using administrative boundaries and roads from Overture Maps (Overture Maps Foundation, 2026). 

Ideally, an up-to-date population count would be available for each building so that clusters can be constructed to accurately contain the correct population size. However, where such detailed and up-to-date information is often unavailable, clusters must be constructed based on estimated building-level population. For this example, in the absence of building-level population data, estimates were created by disaggregating WorldPop gridded population estimates (Bondarenko et al., 2025) across Overture building footprints (Overture Maps Foundation, 2026). Grid cell population estimates were distributed across the buildings according to their footprint area. Larger buildings were therefore assigned a greater share of a grid cell's population, compared to smaller buildings in the same grid cell. This is just one example way to assign population to buildings. Alternative approaches include distributing area-level population estimates evenly across all buildings within each area, or assigning a standard population count to every building across the entire study region.

## Create sampling frame clusters for three example areas

### Load packages

```{r setup}
library(clusterComposer)
library(sf) # load sf for reading in and plotting spatial data 
```

### Locate the example data files

```{r input-directory}
extdata_path <- system.file("extdata", package = "clusterComposer")

```

### Locate directory for output files

```{r output-directory, eval=FALSE}
# set the location for the directory you would like output files to be saved
output_dir <- ""
```


```{r create-output-directory-if-needed}
# create the output folder within this directory, if it does not already exist
output_path <- file.path(output_dir, "output")
dir.create(output_path,recursive = TRUE,showWarnings = FALSE)

```

### Section A: regular road network layout with buildings arranged in clearly defined blocks

Read in the section boundary and buildings data, then plot.

```{r section-a-inputs}
AOI_A <- st_read(file.path(extdata_path, "sectionA.gpkg"))
bf_A <- st_read(file.path(extdata_path, "bfsA.gpkg"))

plot(st_geometry(AOI_A), border = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(st_geometry(bf_A), add = TRUE, col = "grey70", border = "grey40")
```


```{r section-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/Guatemala_sectionA_layout.png")
```

Section A has a regular grid like arrangement of blocks of buildings.

Next, run `clusterComposer` for Section A.

```{r section-a-run}
clusterComposer(
  aoi = AOI_A,
  bf_file_path = file.path(extdata_path, "bfsA.gpkg"),
  run_id = "guatemala_sectionA",
  output_file_path = output_path,
  n_cores = 1
)
```

In these examples, we run `clusterComposer` separately on each section (spatial area) and examine the results. When multiple sections are processed in a single run, `clusterComposer` can use parallel processing, with different sections processed simultaneously by different computing cores. Therefore, we generally recommend using the total number of available cores minus one, although fewer cores can be used. Here, only one section is processed at a time, so we use one core (n_cores = 1).

Now we can read in and plot the sampling frame boundaries produced for Section A. Note that `clusterComposer` saves files as the run_ID plus "_clusters.gpkg". So in this example the file saved is "guatemala_sectionA_clusters.gpkg".

```{r plot-section-results}
# plot the building footprints 
plot(st_geometry(bf_A), col = "grey70", border = "grey40",main = "Section A sampling frame boundaries")

# read in sampling frame units and add to plot
sectionA_boundaries <- st_read(file.path(output_path, "guatemala_sectionA_clusters.gpkg"))
plot(st_geometry(sectionA_boundaries),add = TRUE,col = NA,border = "blue",lwd = 2)

```

```{r clusters-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/Guatemala_sectionA_clusters.png")
```

Now, plot the population sizes of the clusters.

```{r plot-pop-per-cluster}
# clusterComposer calculates the population size for the final cluster boundaries 
# and saves these in a column called "pop"
plot(sectionA_boundaries[,"pop"],main="Section A population size per cluster")

```

```{r pop-per-clusters-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/Guatemala_sectionA_pop_per_clust.png")
```

It will be easier for comparisons across output sampling frames to have standardised population count bands and colour coding. Let's re-plot the population per clusters for section A. 

```{r plot-pop-per-cluster-scale}
sectionA_boundaries$pop_band <- cut(
  sectionA_boundaries[["pop"]],
  breaks = c(-Inf, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, Inf),
  labels = c(
    "≤50", "51–100", "101–150", "151–200",
    "201–250", "251–300", "301–350", ">350"
  ),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

plot(
  sectionA_boundaries["pop_band"],
  pal = c(
    "#ffffcc", "#d9f0a3", "#addd8e", "#78c679",
    "#41ab5d", "#238443", "#006837", "#004529"
  ),
  main = "Section A population size per cluster"
)
```

```{r pop-per-clusters-scale-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/Guatemala_sectionA_pop_per_clust_scale.png")
```

`clusterComposer` has a default target population per cluster of 250 people. In our section A example, `clusterComposer` has successfully generated clusters with populations that are mostly close to this target. `clusterComposer` also has default settings for the maximum and minimum population size per cluster and these govern the range in population sizes across clusters. We will show some results for different population parameters later. First, let's look at two other example urban layouts.

### Section B: buildings arranged in a regular pattern within a more irregular road network

## Create sampling frame clusters with different population parameters

We'll take section A again and create sampling frames for the following population per cluster parameters:

- **Default settings:** target population = 250 people, maximum population = 350 people, minimum population = 150 people
- **Smaller range in population per cluster:** target population = 250 people, maximum population = 300 people, minimum population = 200 people
- **Smaller target population per cluster:** target population = 150 people, maximum population = 200 people, minimum population = 100 people
- **Larger target population per cluster:** target population = 500 people, maximum population = 600 people, minimum population = 400 people

We already created the frame with default settings above. Let's generate frames using the other sets of parameters and then plot the results.

```{r create-sampling-frames-var-pop-paras}
# read in section boundary
AOI_A <- st_read(file.path(extdata_path, "sectionA.gpkg"))

# run clusterComposer for a smaller range of population sizes per cluster
clusterComposer(
  aoi = AOI_A,
  bf_file_path = file.path(extdata_path, "bfsA.gpkg"),
  run_id = "guatemala_sectionA_smallPopRange",
  output_file_path = output_path,
  pop_per_EZ = 250,
  max_pop_per_EZ = 300,
  min_pop_per_EZ = 200,
  n_cores = 1
)

# run clusterComposer for a smaller target population size per cluster
clusterComposer(
  aoi = AOI_A,
  bf_file_path = file.path(extdata_path, "bfsA.gpkg"),
  run_id = "guatemala_sectionA_smallPopTarget",
  output_file_path = output_path,
  pop_per_EZ = 150,
  max_pop_per_EZ = 200,
  min_pop_per_EZ = 100,
  n_cores = 1
)

# run clusterComposer for a larger target population size per cluster
clusterComposer(
  aoi = AOI_A,
  bf_file_path = file.path(extdata_path, "bfsA.gpkg"),
  run_id = "guatemala_sectionA_largePopTarget",
  output_file_path = output_path,
  pop_per_EZ = 500,
  max_pop_per_EZ = 600,
  min_pop_per_EZ = 400,
  n_cores = 1
)

# read in four section A frames
section_boundaries1 <- st_read(file.path(output_path, "guatemala_sectionA_clusters.gpkg"))
section_boundaries2 <- st_read(file.path(output_path, "guatemala_sectionA_smallPopRange_clusters.gpkg"))
section_boundaries3 <- st_read(file.path(output_path, "guatemala_sectionA_smallPopTarget_clusters.gpkg"))
section_boundaries4 <- st_read(file.path(output_path, "guatemala_sectionA_largePopTarget_clusters.gpkg"))

# classify clusters into set population bands
section_boundaries1$pop_band <- cut(section_boundaries1[["pop"]], c(-Inf,100,200,300,400,500,600,Inf), labels = c("≤100","101–200","201–300","301–400","401–500","501–600",">600"))
section_boundaries2$pop_band <- cut(section_boundaries2[["pop"]], c(-Inf,100,200,300,400,500,600,Inf), labels = c("≤100","101–200","201–300","301–400","401–500","501–600",">600"))
section_boundaries3$pop_band <- cut(section_boundaries3[["pop"]], c(-Inf,100,200,300,400,500,600,Inf), labels = c("≤100","101–200","201–300","301–400","401–500","501–600",">600"))
section_boundaries4$pop_band <- cut(section_boundaries4[["pop"]], c(-Inf,100,200,300,400,500,600,Inf), labels = c("≤100","101–200","201–300","301–400","401–500","501–600",">600"))

# plot results
plot(section_boundaries1["pop_band"], pal = rev(hcl.colors(7, "Purples")), main = "Default settings\nTarget population per cluster = 250 (maximum = 350, minimum = 150)", cex.main = 0.7)
plot(section_boundaries2["pop_band"], pal = rev(hcl.colors(7, "Purples")), main = "Smaller range in population per cluster\nTarget population per cluster = 250 (maximum = 300, minimum = 200)", cex.main = 0.7)
plot(section_boundaries3["pop_band"], pal = rev(hcl.colors(7, "Purples")), main = "Smaller target population per cluster\nTarget population per cluster = 150 (maximum = 200, minimum = 100)", cex.main = 0.7)
plot(section_boundaries4["pop_band"], pal = rev(hcl.colors(7, "Purples")), main = "Larger target population per cluster\nTarget population per cluster = 500 (maximum = 600, minimum = 400)", cex.main = 0.7)
```

```{r section-a-pop-paras-figures, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics(c("figures/Guatemala_sectionA_defaultpop.png",
                        "figures/Guatemala_sectionA_smallpoprange.png",
                        "figures/Guatemala_sectionA_smallpop.png",
                        "figures/Guatemala_sectionA_largepop.png"))
```

Using the default population settings, 17 clusters were formed. When the permitted population range was narrowed, 20 clusters were formed, several of which had populations below the minimum of 200. `clusterComposer` treats the maximum as a stricter constraint than the minimum, preferring two clusters below the minimum to one cluster above the maximum.

When the target population was reduced to 150 people, 31 clusters were formed. Most had populations within the specified range of 100–200 people, although a few fell below the minimum. No clusters exceeded the maximum of 200 people.

When the target population was increased to 500 people, just 10 clusters were formed. Five had populations within the specified range, while the other five fell below the minimum. No clusters exceeded the maximum.


## Summary

This vignette provides a guide on how to run `clusterComposer` to create sampling frames for small example areas. It also demonstrates how `clusterComposer` performs across contrasting urban forms and for different population per cluster settings. 

The accuracy of the sampling frames generated by `clusterComposer` depends on the quality of the building footprints and building-level population estimates provided. Users should therefore carefully assess and amend these input data before running `clusterComposer`.
